items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved construction permits on Nov. 9 for four advanced reactors at Dow’s Seadrift chemical complex on the Texas Gulf Coast, a project developed with reactor company X-energy. The units are intended to provide electricity and process heat to the site. The permits do not commit Dow to build or authorize the reactors to operate; Dow expects to consider a preliminary investment decision in 2027, while X-energy forecasts operations in the early 2030s. Regulators and developers point to design features intended to limit accident risks, while Union of Concerned Scientists safety director Edwin Lyman has challenged claims that the fuel is meltdown-proof. The NRC dismissed a local environmental group’s legal challenges to the permit application.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Alberta bill sets data-centre limits and well cleanup funds
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well. Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt. For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing.

items._excerpt: Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well (cbc.ca, nationalobserver.com). Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt (cbc.ca, thestar.com). For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027 (cbc.ca, thestar.com). The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing (boereport.com). Meta project: The Sturgeon County complex is a $13-billion, one-gigawatt development expected to come online in two to three years (cbc.ca). Cleanup backlog: The Orphan Well Association lists 7,328 wells awaiting decommissioning and 9,258 sites needing reclamation; it estimates cleanup costs for its inventory at $1.66 billion (cbc.ca, thestar.com). Emissions cap: Bill 42 would eliminate the oil-sands emissions cap, which set a 100-million-tonne limit and had never been enforced; emissions were about 84 million tonnes in 2023 (boereport.com). Public response: A September CBC-commissioned poll found 31% of Albertans strongly opposed data-centre development and another 26% mostly opposed it, with electricity bills and environmental effects among the concerns (cbc.ca).

items.title: [npr.org] Climate change shifts Arctic greenery, darkens lakes and bleaches coral
items.content_html:

Climate change is altering natural colors across Arctic landscapes, lakes and coral reefs, with shifts linked to warming, permafrost thaw and pollution. Another study found that green-wavelength values in more than 400,000 North American boreal-Arctic lakes fell 15% between 1984 and 2019, indicating darker water. Darker lakes can retain heat longer, while coral bleaching leaves reefs more vulnerable to disease and other stressors. Researchers say thawing permafrost may be darkening lakes as soil mixes into the water.

items.content_html:

A McGill University research centre says a network of nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts has circulated more than 3,201 deepfake videos that drew 22.1 million views over three months. One widely viewed false story described a nonexistent 48-hour ultimatum from President Donald Trump and claimed Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts. It appeared in 161 videos on 129 accounts and drew 5.1 million views. The report says the accounts promote misleading claims from both sides of the trade debate, while the network’s operators and purpose remain unknown. Researchers said posting patterns and some accounts’ Chinese-language settings or registrations in China point to activity outside North America, but they could not firmly attribute the network to anyone. The report says the accounts have not been monetized and could be building an audience for later use, testing a tool or operating on behalf of someone seeking to influence Canadians.

items.title: [nacional.hr] ECDC urges hospital infection controls as resistant infections spread in Europe
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said on Nov. 18 that antibiotic-resistant infections continue to spread in Europe, leaving doctors with fewer effective treatment options. More than 70% of the health burden caused by antimicrobial resistance in Europe is linked to healthcare-associated infections, and stronger infection prevention could avert half of that burden, the ECDC said. The agency called for hand hygiene, protective equipment, prompt detection, isolation of infected patients and effective cleaning in healthcare facilities. It also urged better access to laboratories and adequate infection-control staffing. The ECDC highlighted avoidable antibiotic use for viral illnesses, particularly in children, while Germany’s Robert Koch Institute listed its new ARS-ResistenzCheck data tool among resources for clinical practice.
